A task can wait on a ring buffer for when it fills up to a specific
watermark. The writer will check the minimum watermark that waiters are
waiting for and if the ring buffer is past that
column2: it will wake up all the

column1: waiters.
The waiters are in a wait loop
column2: and will first check if a signal is

column1: pending and then check if the ring buffer is at the desired level where it
should break out of the loop.
If a file that uses a ring buffer closes
the ring buffer
column2: it needs to wake up those threads. To do this

column1: wait_index"" was used.
Before entering the wait loop
column2: the waiter will read the wait_index. On

column1: wakeup
column2: it will check if the wait_index is different than when it entered

column1: the loop
column2: and will exit the loop if it is. The waker will only need to

column1: update the wait_index before waking up the waiters.
This had a couple of bugs. One trivial one and one broken by design.
The trivial bug was that the waiter checked the wait_index after the
schedule() call. It had to be checked between the prepare_to_wait() and
the schedule() which it was not.
The main bug is that the first check to set the default wait_index will
always be outside the prepare_to_wait() and the schedule(). That's because
the ring_buffer_wait() doesn't have enough context to know if it should
break out of the loop.
The loop itself is not needed
column2: because all the callers to the

column1: ring_buffer_wait() also has their own loop
column2: as the callers have a better

column1: sense of what the context is to decide whether to break out of the loop
or not.
Just have the ring_buffer_wait() block once
column2: and if it gets woken up

column1: the function and let the callers decide what to do next.
